pedagogy.summary: This is the LANGUAGE of statistical analysis — mean, median, mode, average, range, frequency, data, sample, outlier, correlation, and the chart words (bar/pie/scatter graph, table). The teaching goal is not reciting definitions but USING each term for the right thing when describing real data. The characteristic difficulty is that these words are 'the distilled wisdom of generations' worn down into everyday speech: 'average' collapses into the add-and-divide rule with no sense of what it represents, the three measures of centre get swapped (the most common value gets called the 'average'; the median is taken before ordering), 'range' is given as the two extreme values rather than their difference, and 'correlation' is used for any relationship and slid into causation. Because 'mean' carries rich colloquial connotations that 'median' and 'mode' lack, children lean on it and leave the others as empty labels. Vocabulary is therefore best built ON real data sets and graphs — name each measure aloud as it is computed, say what it tells us, and contrast the terms on the same data so the words attach to distinct ideas rather than to a single procedure.
bestPractices: Introduce each term ON a real, meaningful data set (goals per match, heights in the class) and immediately ask 'what does this number tell us about the data?', so the word attaches to a meaning, not just a calculation
Contrast mean, median and mode on the SAME data set (especially a skewed one where they differ) so the three words come apart and cannot collapse into 'the average'
Insist that 'range' names ONE number — the difference/spread from lowest to highest — not the two extreme values; show it as a distance
Distinguish 'correlation' as the DIRECTION of a trend (positive/negative/none) between two variables, and keep it explicitly separate from causation ('a link, not a cause')
Use the terms receptively and productively: give the child data and have them narrate it using the words, then listen for correct use rather than asking for definitions

Flag the outlier as a value that doesn't fit the pattern and connect it to its EFFECT (it drags the mean toward it because the mean is influenced by every value), rather than treating it as a mistake to delete
keyRepresentations: A small real data set laid out as an ordered list (so median and mode are visible) alongside its mean and range
A skewed data set where mean, median and mode clearly differ — the canonical way to separate the three terms
A scatter graph showing positive / negative / no correlation for the direction-of-trend vocabulary
A number line marking lowest and highest with the range shown as the distance between them
A word wall / glossary tying each term to a one-line 'what it tells us' and an example
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'average'/mean as only the add-and-divide rule, with no sense of what the number represents about the data
Swapping the measures of centre: calling the most frequent value the 'average', or finding the median without ordering / from the frequency column
Giving 'range' as the two extreme values ('0 and 8') rather than their difference (8)
Using 'correlation' for any relationship and sliding it into causation ('taller people cause bigger feet'), or calling a patternless scatter 'correlated'
Not connecting an outlier to its effect — assuming the mean sits in the middle regardless of an extreme value

learn.summary: Builds the language of statistical analysis (mean, median, mode, range, outlier, correlation, plus data/sample/frequency and chart words) for 9–11 year-olds by attaching each term to what it tells us about real data, not to a recited definition or a single add-and-divide rule. The core teaching move is contrasting the three measures of centre on the SAME data set — especially a skewed one — so 'mean', 'median' and 'mode' come apart instead of collapsing into 'the average', naming range as ONE number (a distance), tying 'outlier' to its pull on the mean, and keeping 'correlation' as direction-of-trend distinct from causation. Activities span a draggable live data set (primary builder of meaning), use-in-context narration, categorisation/matching checks, an in-role data detective, and a static glossary reference — each with a different pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Draggable data set: watch the measures behave differently
feedback: When the mean chases the dragged value while the median stays put: 'The mean is pulled by every value, so an extreme score drags it — the median, the middle after ordering, barely moves.'
If the child expects all three to move together: 'Notice the mode didn't change at all and the median stayed at 2 — only the mean (and the range) moved. These words name different things.'
On the range strip: 'The range is the gap you can see — one number, the distance from lowest to highest, not the two end values.'
On the scatter: 'That's positive correlation — taller tends to go with bigger feet. It's a link, not proof that one makes the other happen.'
activities.rationale: Statistical vocabulary attaches to meaning when the words are tied to data the child manipulates and sees respond. Live, simultaneous recomputation of mean/median/mode/range as a value is dragged makes visible which word tracks what — the specific difficulty that 'average' collapses into a procedure and the three centres get swapped. The interactive affordance (dragging, live relabelling, a correlation slider) makes the mechanism concrete; it is one strong way to separate the terms, not the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding: students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors, and the mean is influenced by every value (so adding an extreme value shifts it); a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed

Russell & Mokros classified students' notions of average into 'most frequent value/mode', 'reasonable value', 'midpoint' and 'algorithmic relationship'; and Barr found students confused about what the median is the 'middle' of (the values, the frequency column, or the unordered list)

'Correlation' refers to association/co-variation between two quantitative variables and does NOT imply cause and effect; people show 'illusory correlation', overestimating association when they believe a causal link exists; the intuitive notion of variability is 'unalikeability' — how much values differ from each other
learnerActions: Start with a small, meaningful data set shown as dots on a value strip — e.g. goals a team scored across seven matches: 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2, 8 (ordered: 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 8, so the mode is a single clear value, 2).
Read the mean, median, mode and range displayed and labelled live beside the data, each with a one-line 'what it tells us'.
Drag one match's score (say the 3) up to 20 and watch the mean slide up to chase it, the median barely move, and the mode stay unchanged — the moment the three labelled numbers behave DIFFERENTLY.
Drag a value far from the rest to create an outlier, then recompute the mean with and without it and compare how little the median shifts.
See the range marked on a number line as the labelled distance from lowest to highest, so it reads as one number, not two.

Switch to a scatter panel (e.g. height vs shoe size) and move a correlation slider from negative through none to positive, labelled as the trend's direction, with a standing caption 'a link, not a cause'.
activities.intendedInsight: Mean, median and mode are not interchangeable words for 'average': they track different things, and seeing them respond differently to the same change is what pulls the words apart. The mean is influenced by every value, so an outlier drags it while the median hardly moves; range is a single distance; correlation names the direction of a trend, not a cause.

activities.title: Narrate the data: use the words for the right thing
feedback: If the child restates the calculation when asked what the mean tells us: 'That's how you find it — but if the team scored this average every match, how many is that? The mean is a typical / fair-share score.'

If the mode is called the 'average' or the median given from the unordered list: say each word aloud as its value is found, ordering the list first for the median, so the three attach to three distinct things.
If the range is given as '0 and 8': 'Can a range be two numbers? Mark both ends on a number line — the range is the gap between them, 8.'
If the outlier is spotted but disconnected: recompute the mean with and without the 8 and compare to the median, tying 'outlier' to its pull on the mean.
If correlation is read as cause: offer a link-not-cause counterexample (ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer) so 'correlation' names co-variation, not causation.
activities.rationale: Checking use in context — productive narration with responsive probing — tests whether the words carry meaning, which definition recall does not. The probes are targeted at the documented confusions (average-as-procedure, swapped centres, range-as-extremes, outlier-mean link, correlation-vs-cause).
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding: students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors, and the mean is influenced by every value (so adding an extreme value shifts it); a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed

In school years 4-6, pupils primarily express procedural knowledge and sometimes mix up the definitions of mean and median; 'mean' carries everyday colloquial connotations that 'median' and 'mode' lack (median is seen as only existing in school), so the latter are harder to explain

'Correlation' refers to association/co-variation between two quantitative variables and does NOT imply cause and effect; people show 'illusory correlation', overestimating association when they believe a causal link exists; the intuitive notion of variability is 'unalikeability' — how much values differ from each other
learnerActions: Take a small real data set — e.g. 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2, 8 — and a scatter graph of height against shoe size, and tell the story of the data aloud using mean, median, mode and range as you go.

For each term, say not just the value but what it tells us: the mode is the most frequent value (2, appearing three times); the median is the middle AFTER ordering (2); the mean (≈2.57) is a typical / fair-share score; the range is 8, the difference 8−0.
Name the 8 as an outlier and say what it does — it drags the mean UP while the median barely moves.
Describe the scatter with the right word: 'positive correlation' meaning taller children tend to have bigger feet — a link, not a cause.

Answer follow-up probes: 'What does that 2.57 actually tell us about how this team scores?'; 'Why did you have to order the numbers for the median but not the mode?'; 'If that 8 had been 80, which number would change most and which hardly at all?'; 'Does being tall MAKE feet grow, or is there a word for the link without saying one causes the other?'
activities.intendedInsight: Owning the vocabulary means using each word for the thing it names when describing freely — not reciting definitions. Narrating real data exposes and corrects swaps (mode called 'average', range given as two numbers, correlation slid into cause) that a definition task would let a child recite around.

activities.title: Match and sort: check correct use, not definitions
feedback: If the 'range = two extremes' sentence is picked: 'Range is one number — the difference. The two end values are the extremes, a different thing.'
If a patternless scatter is sorted as 'positive' or 'negative': 'No clear trend means no correlation — correlation is about the direction of a trend.'
If the mode is matched to the 'average' slot: 'The most frequent value is the mode; the mean is the add-and-divide typical value — different words.'
activities.rationale: Selected-response and matching items keep every item anchored to a data context and avoid 'define X', so they assess use rather than recall. This is a complement to construction, not a substitute for it: recognition items do not by themselves elicit the independent narration that shows ownership.
sourceClaims: Russell & Mokros classified students' notions of average into 'most frequent value/mode', 'reasonable value', 'midpoint' and 'algorithmic relationship'; and Barr found students confused about what the median is the 'middle' of (the values, the frequency column, or the unordered list)
learnerActions: On a given ordered data set, match each word — mean, median, mode, range — to the value it names.
Sort a set of scatter graphs into positive / negative / no correlation.
Choose which sentence uses 'range' correctly, where a distractor names the two extreme values ('0 and 8') instead of their difference (8).
Judge statements as 'uses the word correctly' or 'incorrectly' (e.g. 'the median is the middle of the unordered list', 'the mode is the average').
activities.intendedInsight: Correct use can be probed by matching and categorising against a data context — this surfaces swaps without asking the child to recite a definition.

activities.title: Data detective: catch the swap in conversation
feedback: Character confirms correct use: 'Yes — the mode is the most common score, and you named it right.'
Character queries a misuse: 'You called the most common value the average — is that the mode or the mean?'
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue draws the child into using the terms and can query misuse responsively. It supports USE rather than building the underlying meaning, because conversation alone cannot compute the measures or show them move as data changes — best as a follow-on to hands-on data work, not the primary builder.
sourceClaims: In school years 4-6, pupils primarily express procedural knowledge and sometimes mix up the definitions of mean and median; 'mean' carries everyday colloquial connotations that 'median' and 'mode' lack (median is seen as only existing in school), so the latter are harder to explain
learnerActions: Take on a 'data detective' role: a character presents a data story and asks the child to describe it.
Describe the data aloud, choosing the right statistical words.
Respond when the character echoes back correct usage or queries a misuse — e.g. 'You said the range is 0 and 8 — can a range be two numbers?'
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through a data story and being gently pressed on word choice surfaces swaps in the moment and rehearses precise use.

activities.title: Glossary reference: anchor each term to its meaning
feedback: Each card restates the meaning plainly: e.g. 'Range: one number — the distance from lowest to highest.'
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference anchors each term to a meaning and example and is useful alongside active work. Because it is fixed, it cannot show the measures respond to changing data — the very contrast that separates the terms — so it serves as a reference, not as the builder of use.
learnerActions: On a fixed, annotated data set, reveal cards for 'mean', 'median', 'mode', 'range' and 'outlier', each giving what it names and a one-line 'what it tells us' with an example.
Use the glossary as a reference while working on the other activities.
activities.intendedInsight: Each term is tied to a one-line meaning and an example, giving a stable reference point for the vocabulary.

constraints: Teach each term ON a real, meaningful data set and immediately ask 'what does this number tell us about the data?', so the word attaches to a meaning rather than to a calculation.

Contrast mean, median and mode on the SAME data set — ideally a skewed one where they differ — so the three words cannot collapse into 'the average'. When demonstrating mode, use a data set with a single clear most-frequent value to avoid bimodal ambiguity.
Order the list before finding the median; make clear the median is the middle of the ordered values, not the unordered list or the frequency column.
'Range' names ONE number — the difference/spread from lowest to highest (e.g. 8−0 = 8) — shown as a distance, never given as the two extreme values.
Keep 'correlation' as the direction of a trend (positive/negative/none) and explicitly separate from causation ('a link, not a cause'); do not call a patternless scatter 'correlated'.
Treat the outlier as a value that doesn't fit the pattern and connect it to its EFFECT (it pulls the mean because the mean is influenced by every value), not as a mistake to delete.

Assess by listening for correct USE in free description, not by asking for definitions; recognition/matching items check use against a data context but do not by themselves show independent construction.

Observable affordances/limits, not claims of medium superiority: the static glossary cannot show the measures respond to changing data, and the in-role conversation cannot compute the measures or show them move as data changes. The live data manipulation can display the measures behaving differently as a value is dragged, and narration on the same data can also contrast the terms; no single medium is universally required to build meaning.
A third spatial dimension is unnecessary for 1D data sets and 2D scatter relationships and risks obscuring the terms; prefer the 1D strip and 2D scatter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.
Original assess states 'range = 7 (the difference 8−0, one number)', which is internally inconsistent because 8−0 = 8. All learner-facing text here uses the correct value, range = 8.

Original example 2,0,1,3,2,1,8 is bimodal (1 and 2 each appear twice) yet the source asserts a unique mode = 2 and mean ≈ 2.4 (17/7 ≈ 2.43). To give a clean single-mode demonstration, the data set was adjusted to 2,0,1,3,2,2,8 (ordered 0,1,2,2,2,3,8): mode = 2 (three times), median = 2, range = 8, mean = 18/7 ≈ 2.57. This mean differs from the original correctAnswer's ≈2.4; reviewers should confirm the intended data set and reconcile the saved assess fields.

'High' confidence and any claim that static or conversational media 'cannot build meaning' are not independently verified; these were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements, and no comparative efficacy of media is established by the sources.

probeDeeper: 'You said the mean is about 2.4 — what does that 2.4 actually tell us about how this team scores?' — pushes 'average' from procedure to meaning
'Why did you have to put the numbers in order to find the median, but not to find the mode?' — forces the distinction between the terms into the open

Counterexample: 'If that 8 had been 80 instead, which of your numbers — mean, median, mode, range — would change the most, and which would hardly move?' — tests outlier/spread vocabulary on a fresh case
'Taller children here tend to have bigger feet — does being tall MAKE feet grow? What word describes the link without saying one causes the other?' — probes correlation-vs-cause
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE: mode = 2 (most frequent), median = 2 (the middle AFTER ordering), mean ≈ 2.4 and a sense of what it represents (a fair-share / typical score), range = 7 (the difference 8−0, one number), the 8 named as an outlier that pulls the mean UP (because the mean is influenced by every value) while the median barely moves, and the scatter described with 'positive correlation' meaning taller children tend to have bigger feet — a link, not stated as a cause. Terms used precisely and for the right thing is mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Average' as bare procedure: uses 'average'/'mean' only for the add-and-divide calculation and cannot say what the resulting number represents about the data
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by pressing for meaning: 'if the team scored this average every match, how many is that?' — tie the mean to a fair-share / typical value on the actual data, so the word carries a meaning, not just a rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child computes the mean but, asked what it tells us, restates the calculation ('you add them and divide') rather than what it says about the team's scoring

errorPatterns.pattern: Swapping the measures of centre: calls the most frequent value the 'average'/'mean', or gives the median without ordering (or from the frequency column) — the three terms collapse into one
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast all three on this same data set, saying each word aloud as its value is found (order the list first for the median), so mean, median and mode attach to three distinct things
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child labels the mode as the 'average', or names a 'median' that is the middle of the UNORDERED list, using the wrong word for the value they found

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Range' as the extremes, not their difference: gives the range as the two end values ('0 and 8') rather than the single number 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that 'range' names ONE number — the distance from lowest to highest — by marking both ends on a number line and showing the gap; contrast 'what are the extremes?' with 'what is the range?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked for the range, the child says two numbers (the lowest and highest) instead of computing and stating their difference

errorPatterns.pattern: Outlier disconnected from its effect: names the 8 as odd but does not connect it to the mean, assuming the mean sits in the middle regardless of an extreme value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the mean is influenced by every value: recompute the mean with and without the 8 (and compare to the median, which barely moves), so 'outlier' is tied to its pull on the mean
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child spots the 8 as unusual but, asked what it does to the mean, says it makes no difference or that the mean is 'in the middle' — not that it drags the mean up

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Correlation' used loosely or as causation: applies 'correlation' to any relationship, calls a patternless scatter 'correlated', or reads it as one variable causing the other
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate correlation from cause explicitly: describe the trend's DIRECTION (positive/negative/none) and offer a link-not-cause counterexample (ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer) so 'correlation' names co-variation, not causation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the scatter the child says 'being tall makes your feet bigger', or uses 'correlation' for a scatter with no trend, rather than naming the direction of the trend as a link

responseLevels.gap: Swaps the terms when describing — the most common value is called the 'average', the range comes out as two numbers, 'correlation' is used for any link or not at all; the words are labels without attached meanings
responseLevels.full: In an unprompted description of a fresh data set, uses mean, median, mode, range, outlier and correlation precisely and for the right thing — says what each tells us, notes the outlier's pull on the mean, and keeps correlation distinct from causation
responseLevels.partial: Uses each term correctly when prompted one at a time, but in free description reverts to 'average' loosely, cannot say what a measure represents, or does not spontaneously flag the outlier's effect or keep correlation distinct from cause — lists the terms without coordinating them on real data

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small real data set — e.g. goals a team scored in seven matches: 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 8 — and a simple scatter graph of, say, height against shoe size for the class. Set a talking task, NOT a definition task: 'Tell me the story of this team's scoring — use the words mean, median, mode and range as you go, and say what each one tells us. There's an 8 in there: what would you call that value, and what does it do to the mean? Now look at this scatter graph and describe the relationship using the right word.' Listen for which terms they USE and whether each is used for the right thing. (Do not ask 'what does mean/range/correlation mean?' — listen for correct USE in the description.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who owns the vocabulary attaches each word to a distinct thing when describing freely; a child holding only labels reveals it the moment they describe — the most common value gets called 'the average', the range comes out as 'nought and eight', 'correlation' is used for any link or slid into 'taller makes your feet grow'. Narrating real data exposes swaps that a term-by-term definition quiz would let the child recite around.
